source.title: Learning Rates as a Function of Batch Size: A Random Matrix Theory Approach to Neural Network Training
source.authors: Diego Granziol; Stefan Zohren; Stephen J. Roberts

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some equations and figure content appear garbled in the supplied extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies batch size and optimizer and reports training and validation/test performance under different learning-rate scaling rules, using its own experimental setup.
record.gate_note: Results cited from prior work, including the random-label memorization finding, are not this study's results. Hessian spectra and initialization distance are measured, but the study does not test the magnitude-aware perturbation measure in V7.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own held-out performance comparisons across batch sizes, learning-rate scaling rules and optimizers, bearing directly on V5 and V4. Its Hessian measurements do not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly correct but should state the assumptions and damping condition. Under their spiked random-matrix model, the authors derive batch-Hessian spectral broadening and recommend, up to a threshold, linear learning-rate scaling for SGD and square-root scaling for Adam with small damping. They validate these prescriptions primarily on VGG-16/CIFAR-100 and additionally validate SGD scaling on WideResNet/CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-32. They also recommend using batch rather than empirical curvature when learning rates and momentum are estimated from curvature.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates batch-Hessian spectra and learning-rate scaling, not the original claim's random-label memorization/generalization experiments or the other listed interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, optimizer, learning-rate scaling rule, batch normalization, weight decay, damping, architecture, and dataset are shown to affect results.

fits_no_version.finding: Mini-batching broadens Hessian and generalized Gauss–Newton spectra, with larger extremal eigenvalues.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size changes estimated curvature and the largest stable learning rate; these spectral measurements do not establish V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed B=1024, a larger learning rate gives better test accuracy and greater distance from initialization despite slightly worse training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate choice and initialization distance correlate with held-out performance in this setting; initialization distance is not V7's sharpness measure.

fits_no_version.finding: Data augmentation raises VGG-16 CIFAR-100 test accuracy from 48.8% to 72.1% under the same schedule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation improves accuracy in this experiment; dropout and weight-decay removal are not tested.

record.problems: The principal scaling results are mostly conveyed through figures and qualitative descriptions without numerical final-error values. Batch-size comparisons change the learning rate with batch size, so they do not isolate a fixed-recipe batch penalty. The authors acknowledge finite-size stochasticity and that their theory assumes a random-matrix model; they note that batch-normalization dependence is not fully analyzed.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows were identified. Cited results from other studies and Hessian-spectrum measurements that do not directly measure the versions' stated outcomes were excluded.

untested.parts: No paired natural-label and random-label training experiment; random-label fitting is cited.
No width sweep beyond the width required for interpolation.
No convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance comparison or local-connectivity intervention.

No controlled restriction to learning-rate and decay-schedule tuning, broad optimizer benchmark, language-model comparison, or Adam-to-SGD switching experiment. Decoupled weight decay is not isolated as an intervention.
No language-model experiment, longer-training intervention, warmup comparison, or isolated normalization/regularization rescue. Batch size and learning rate change together.
No dropout intervention or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
No magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation measure, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal and retraining comparison for memorized versus random examples.

missing.what: Appendix F quantifies recipe sensitivity at B=1024: linear scaling with learning rate 0.08 gives validation accuracy 64.35% and test error 34.64%; square-root scaling with learning rate 0.028 gives 61.08% and 37.55%. The B=128 validation baseline is 65.82%. Add rows for these comparisons.

Figure 31(a–b) compares ImageNet ResNet-50 training and held-out curves for SGD and AdamW at several damping settings. The authors explicitly report closure of the optimizer generalization gap with appropriate damping. Add the qualitative comparison, preserving the figure's AdamW designation and the absence of numerical default-Adam accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for the listed versions. Failure of an alternative scaling rule does not itself challenge V5, which already allows recipe dependence and workload-dependent thresholds. The supplied text supports no challenge verdict against V4 or V5 as written. Figure-only results with unreadable condition-specific values should remain qualitative.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization are cited as prior work, not tested here.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison is reported.
The study compares SGD, Adam, Adam with increased damping, and KFAC on its own settings; it does not report a broad optimizer benchmark or systematic tuning-budget comparison.
The study varies batch size with learning-rate scaling under its stated schedules; it does not isolate a general fixed-epoch penalty across arbitrary recipes or language models.
The study measures Hessian spectra and discusses sharpness, but does not test magnitude-aware weight perturbations or rank that measure against generalization gaps.
No memorized-example removal experiment is reported.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Varied batch size and proportionally scaled the initial SGD learning rate.
rows.value: Training and validation accuracy remains stable until a small drop for B=1024, a larger drop for B=2048, and no training for B=4096.
rows.note: The study holds its 300-epoch budget and adapts learning rate linearly with batch size; this is not an unadapted fixed-recipe comparison.
rows.check: Split the condition groups: performance remains stable through B=512, deteriorates slightly at B=1024 and more at B=2048, and training fails at B=4096. The combined row mixes successful recipe adaptation with a remaining large-batch penalty.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Varied batch size and proportionally scaled the initial SGD learning rate.
rows.value: The authors report a similar pattern of stable performance under linear scaling up to a threshold.
rows.note: Results are described qualitatively; plotted values are not transcribed as numbers.
rows.check: Figure 14 includes B=1024, 2048 and 4096 as well as B=16–512. Restore these conditions and separate stable performance from threshold failure. The caption's wording about no weight decay conflicts with its nonzero coefficient; Section 10.1 confirms weight decay is used.

rows.subject: WideResNet-28 × 10
rows.operation_detail: Varied batch size with a fixed learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio under SGD.
rows.value: Training and test performance is stable for a variety of learning rates with fixed learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio, up to a threshold; highly unstable oscillatory trajectories converge after learning-rate reduction but do not reach peak performance.
rows.note: Includes an explicit qualification about unstable trajectories.
rows.check: Separate stable scaled runs from unstable trajectories with inferior final performance. The prose does not identify the precise batch-size threshold or provide numerical final errors.

rows.subject: WideResNet-28 × 10
rows.operation_detail: Varied batch size with a fixed learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio under SGD.
rows.value: The authors describe the scaling pattern as consistent for this setting.
rows.note: The figure does not provide transcribed final values.
rows.check: The stated 40-epoch budget is inconsistent with Figure 16's final-epoch insets around epochs 47–49, indicating approximately 50 epochs. The text supports consistency up to a threshold but does not identify condition-specific final errors.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Varied batch size and scaled Adam's initial learning rate with the square root of batch size.
rows.measure: Training and validation error; test error consistency is also described in the text
rows.value: The authors report excellent agreement down to B=16, with very small differences between training curves and validation performance; B=8 shows slight training instability.
rows.note: The text says test-error estimates are consistent throughout the range, but gives no corresponding numerical values here.
rows.check: The large-batch held-out penalty is absent under this adapted recipe; that supports V5's adaptation clause. Correct the learning-rate rule to 0.0004√(B/128), using the experimental prose and baseline. The figure caption contains an inconsistent coefficient, and its B=1024 legend also differs from the exact rule. B=8 instability concerns a smaller batch.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Applied square-root learning-rate scaling to SGD as a comparison.
rows.value: Square-root scaling for SGD does not hold; the authors report poor training and divergence.
rows.note: This is an optimizer-specific comparison to the proposed Adam scaling rule.
rows.check: Poor training and divergence when reducing batch size with an unsuitable scaling rule do not establish a reversed held-out batch-size effect. The supplied prose does not specify final validation comparisons for these conditions. Retain as a batch-recipe comparison, with its outcome direction unresolved.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Applied linear learning-rate scaling to Adam as a comparison.
rows.measure: Training and validation error; test error
rows.value: The text reports rapid divergence upon doubling batch size and significant test-error increases as the learning rate is reduced under this scaling; stated test errors are 38.1% ± 0.4, 37.6% ± 0.64, 38% ± 0.25, 40.1% ± 0.3, and 42.7% ± 0.1.
rows.uncertainty: The reported test-error values include ± values as stated.
rows.note: The five test-error values are stated together without an explicit mapping to individual batch sizes, so no such mapping is assigned.
rows.check: The row combines opposite condition groups: increasing batch size produces divergence, while reducing batch size and learning rate worsens test error among convergent runs. Split these groups. The five test errors lack an explicit batch-size mapping and cannot justify a single reversed state.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Compared test accuracy for SGD, Adam-D (Adam with increased damping), and Adam.
rows.note: Adam-D is close to SGD; Adam is lower in this comparison.
rows.check: Split standard Adam from Adam with tuned damping. Standard Adam's 61.9±0.4 versus SGD's 65.3±0.6 shows the disadvantage; Adam-D's 65.5±0.7 shows recovery to comparable accuracy. The table does not establish that only learning rates and decay schedules were tuned.

source_check.correct: Split optimizer conditions: standard Adam, 61.9 ± 0.4 versus SGD, 65.3 ± 0.6, has state observed; Adam-D, 65.5 ± 0.7 versus the same SGD baseline, has state absent for the adaptive-optimizer disadvantage.
